originalTitle: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
summary: CoreWeave had a bad week last week. content: CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too. Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else. To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more. “The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying. I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit. CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year. So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue. Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business. Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one. Anyway, some people are buying the dip.
chineseTitle: CoreWeave的债务正在成为整个 AI 行业的问题
chineseSummary: CoreWeave 上周过得很糟糕。根据一个常见的定义，当投资者要求的收益率比他们从政府债券中获得的收益高出 1,000 个基点时，其债券就陷入了困境。上周二，查马斯“SPAC之王”帕里哈皮蒂亚注意到了不良债务，并询问人工智能的建设是否是私人信贷泡沫。 […]
chineseContent: CoreWeave 上周过得很糟糕。根据一个常见的定义，当投资者要求的收益率比他们从政府债券中获得的收益高出 1,000 个基点时，其债券就陷入了困境。上周二，查马斯“SPAC之王”帕里哈皮蒂亚注意到了不良债务，并询问人工智能的建设是否是私人信贷泡沫。自周二收盘以来，其股价已下跌超过 20%，跌幅相当大！市场上的其他人工智能公司似乎也受到了一些附带损害。现在，我还问过人工智能行业是否存在泡沫，但当 SPAC 之王回应了一位女士的担忧时，这位女士一直对人工智能提出的问题是“冠军们，我们计划如何负担得起这个费用？”，这是一个非常不同的信号。当我说“哎呀”时，这是一回事。当埃隆·马斯克这么说时，那就是另一回事了。让 CoreWeave 的情况变得更糟的是，该公司的联合创始人之一布兰宁·麦克比 (Brannin McBee) 在上周（与帕里哈皮蒂亚发帖的同一天）向英国《金融时报》表示，该公司希望其债务达到投资级，而不是垃圾级，这样它就可以从保险公司借款，因为用他的话说，保险公司的资本是“无限的”。这并非完全不合理——今年早些时候，CoreWeave 获得了第一笔投资级芯片贷款。但当你谈到想要利用保险公司拥有的巨额资金时，投资者就会担心 CoreWeave（已经是一个庞大的债务人）会借更多的钱。彭博社援引大都会人寿投资管理公司杠杆融资联席主管约翰·约万诺维奇的话说：“问题不在于去年的信用状况发生了变化，而在于我们还有一年半的供应。”我看到有人认为这意味着人工智能泡沫正在到来
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于 AI 与科技趋势信号，适合用于观察工具选型、产品机会、开发者关注点和技术路线变化。
